newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan stocks hit 1996 high, but analysts cautious.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan stocks hit 1996 high, but analysts cautious.

text.p: Taiwan share prices closed at a high for the year on Monday on active buying of plastic and textile issues, but securities analysts cautioned that it was too early for long-term optimism.
"I am a little bit surprised by today's good performance," said Oliver Fang, an analyst at National Securities.
The weighted index ended 63.62 points or 0.96 percent higher at 6,659.72, the highest closing level in 1996.
Brokers attributed Monday's rise in part to a bank's bullish projection of soaring profits for giant Formosa Plastics group, which fuelled wider buying.

The China Times quoted a Tokyo-Mitsubishi Bank report as saying Formosa Plastics group's US$9 billion petrochemical project, to open in 1999, would boost the conglomerate into one of the island's best long-term investments.
The study predicted that profits for the group's three key members -- Formosa Plastics, Nan Ya Plastics and Formosa Chemical and Fiber -- would soar in 2000.
All three closed sharply higher on active buying.
"The (Formosa Plastics) report is the main reason for the rise," said Chen Han-chung, an analyst of Yungli Securities.
"But I don't think the market will rise too much or too fast because of the report. Lots of things can happen between now the the year 2000," Chen added.
Recent record-high margin loans outstanding and institutional investors' year-end window-dressing might deter further sharp gains, analysts said.
Some analysts said the index was likely to encounter strong resistance at around 6,700 points, with different sectors taking turns to rise and support the market.

The government's stimulus measures engineered by President Lee Teng-hui after his May 20 inauguration have helped fuel stock market sentiment described by analysts as bullish but also somewhat speculative.
Lee, who won in a landslide in the island's first direct presidential election, has demanded that all government agencies act to boost investment in the second half of 1996.
"Many investors are pinning their hopes on more government actions before Lee's six-month deadline (on November 20)," said Norman Lee, an analyst of Foremost Investment Services.

"Some people even believe the government will offer a new olive branch to ease long-strained relations with communist China," Lee said, adding that President Lee's renewed invitation to China's leaders to visit Taiwan was taken as a positive sign.
"Of course it is only wishful thinking, but you cannot stop people from being optimistic at the moment," Norman Lee said.
"Just keep in mind that a bull run cannot be sustained by speculative buying."
China has regarded Taiwan as a Chinese province not entitled to foreign ties since a civil war separated them in 1949.
A political impasse between Taiwan and China started in June 1995 after President Lee made a private visit to the United States, which Beijing saw as a move to promote independence.
After the visit, Beijing suspended semi-official talks with Taipei and launched a military intimidation campaign, which peaked ahead of Taiwan's March 23 presidential election.
